## Overview

This guide contains a brief summary of how to extend various initial models to account for transients. Three initial models of increasing complexity are considered:

1.  A single-state Cormack-Jolly-Seber model.
2.  A multi-state model of survival and movement between two sites (thus a multi-site model).
3.  A multi-state model of survival and movement between two sites, incorporating trap-dependence.

For each of these examples we briefly present a Stan implementation of the initial models, before explaining the changes in data preparation and Stan code that are required to accomodate transients.



### Product-multinomial likelihoods 

Our approach to incorporating transients is computationally advantageous when the
initial model has a fast product-multinomial likelihood for a reduced data representation
known as an 'm-array'. The most complex parts of the code are those that calculate 
the cell probabilities for these multinomial likelihoods in terms of e.g. survival and 
detection probabilities. For readers unfamiliar with these we refer to Williams 
et al.

Package in functions ... could explain a bit about those functions?

### Parameter structure
We consider time-varying survival, detection and residency probabilities,
but time-constant movement probabilities.

## Single-state Cormack-Jolly-Seber model

The model has a single live state, and the capture histories can be summarised
by the number of individuals released on occasion $s$ that are next recapture on
occasion $t$, or never recaptured. 

### The initial model without transients

#### Preparing the data in R

From the capture history matrix one summarises the data as an m-array. We have 
written our own function to do this, `get_marray`, but others are available, 
e.g. in R2ucare. In the single-state case the m-array is a $T-1 \times T$ matrix,
where $T$ are the number of sampling occasions. 

#### Stan code

The trickiest part to coding the model is calculating the cell probabilities for
the multinomial distributions. We bundle this into a function `get_multinomial_probs`
in the `functions` code block. The rest is, hopefully, quite self explanatory:


```stan
functions {
  matrix get_multinomial_probs( data int T, vector p, vector phi ) { 
  // ... function body ...
  }
}

data {
  int<lower=2> T;                     // number of years
  array[T-1, T] int<lower=0> marr;    // m-array 
}

parameters {
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T] p;         // detection probability
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T-1] phi;     // survival probability
} 

model {
  // multinomial probabilities
  matrix[T-1, T] pr;      
  pr = get_multinomial_probs(T, p ,phi);
  
  // priors
  p ~ beta(1,1);
  phi ~ beta(1,1);
  
  // likelihood
  for (t in 1:(T - 1)) {
    marr[t] ~ multinomial(pr[t]');
  }
}
```


In Stan, a single index into a matrix (e.g. `marr[t]`) returns the relevant *row*
of the matrix. The prime in `multinomial(pr[t]')` transposes the row vector `pr[t]` 
to give a vector which is accepted by the mutinomial distribution. 


### Extending the model to account for transients

Now we consider the extension to account for transients. In the 'initial' model
all individuals are assumed to be residents. 

#### Preparing the data in R

The following steps are required to prepare the data for the extended product-multinomial 
likelihood. 

i. Split the capture histories into single-encounter and
multiple-encounter histories.
ii. Construct an m-array from the multiple-encounter capture histories alone.
iii. Count the number of single-encounter and multiple-encounter capture histories in each 
cohort. 

#### Stan code

Fortunately, the most complicated part of the Stan code, namely the function
`get_multinomial_probs` requires no changes, so the functions code block remains
unchanged.

In the data block, we add the counts of single- and multi-encounter capture histories
for each cohort. 

:::{.callout-caution}
The m-array here must be constructed from *only* multiple-encounter capture
histories. This is easy to forget as the Stan code declaring the m-array is unchanged 
from the initial model. 
:::

In the extended model the data block becomes

```stan
data {
  int<lower=2> T;                      // number of years
   array[T-1, T] int<lower=0> marr;    // m-array from multi-encounter histories only 
   array[T-1] int<lower=0> Nsingle;    // no. single encounter histories per cohort 
   array[T-1] int<lower=0> Nmult;      // no. multiple encounter histories per cohort
}
```

The parameters block needs only have the residency probabilities added to it:
```stan
parameters {
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T] p;         // detection probability for 'residents'
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T-1] phi;     // survival probability
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T-1] pi_r;    // proportion 'residents' in each cohort
}
```

In the model block one adds priors for the new parameters, and increments the
log-posterior with the extra terms resulting from transients:
```stan
model {
  // multinomial probabilities
  matrix[T-1, T] pr;
  pr = get_multinomial_probs(T, p ,phi);

 // priors
  p ~ beta(1,1);
  phi ~ beta(1,1);
  pi_r ~ beta(1,1);
  
  // likelihood...
  // ... for indiv recaptured at least once
  for (t in 1:(T-1)) {
    marr[t] ~ multinomial(pr[t]');
    target += Nmult[t] * log(pi_r[t]); 
  }
  // ... for indiv never recaptured
  for (t in 1:(T-1)) {
    target += Nsingle[t] * log( pr[t][T] * pi_r[t] + (1 - pi_r[t]) );
  }
}
```

In the likelihood for single-encounter capture histories, `pr[t][T]` contains
the probability that an individual released at time $t$ is never recaptured, given
that they are resident. 

## Multi-state model 

The multi-state model we consider is a multi-site model with two sites, in which
we model site-dependent survival, detection and movement. Now the m-array summarises
the capture histories by the number of individuals released on occasion $s$ in state $i$
that are next recaptured on occasion $t$ in state $j$, or never recaptured. Since
there are two states the m-array has dimensions $2(T-1) \times 2(T-1)+1$.

### The initial model without transients

#### Preparing the data in R

In R one constructs the multi-state m-array.

#### Stan code

The structure of the Stan code is very similar to the single-state model (without transients),
except that the function to compute multinomial cell probabilities is a little more complicated.
Treating the contents of the function as a black box for now, the Stan code is:

```stan
functions {
  matrix get_multinomial_probs(
    data int T,
    array[] vector p,
    array[] vector phi,
    array[] vector m
  ) {
    // ... function body ...
  }
}

data {
  int<lower=2> T;                                 // number of years
  array[2*(T-1), 2*(T-1)+1] int<lower=0> marr;    // m-array
}

parameters {
  array[2] vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T] p;      // detection probabilities
  array[2] vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T-1] phi;  // survival probabilities
  array[2] simplex[2] m;                      // movement probabilities 
}

model {
  // calculate multinomial probabilities
  matrix[2*(T-1), 2*(T-1)+1] pr;
  pr = get_multinomial_probs( T, p, phi, m );
  // m-array capture-recapture likelihood
  for (i in 1:(2*(T-1))) {
    marr[i] ~ multinomial(pr[i]');
  }
}
```
Here we have coded the survival and detection parameters' dependence on sites using 
an array of vectors. For example, `phi` is an array with two elements, `phi[1]` 
is a vector of survival probabilities at site 1 for occasions $t = 1, \cdots, T-1$,
and `phi[2]` contains those for site 2. The movement probabilities are conditional
on survival, thus they must sum to one for each source site. Stan's simplex data
type conveniently handles this constraint. Thus `m[1]` is a simplex (a vector of non-negative
reals that sums to one) that stores the probabilities that an individual that survives at 
site $1$ will remain at that site or move to site $2$.


### Extending the model to account for transients

The extension to include transients requires the same types of moves as it did in
the the single-state case.

#### Preparing the data in R

The following steps are required to prepare the data for the extended product-multinomial 
likelihood. These are the same as in the single-state case, except for the last step.

i. Split the capture histories into single-encounter and
multiple-encounter histories.
ii. Construct an m-array from the multiple-encounter capture histories alone.
iii. Count the number of single-encounter and multiple-encounter capture histories 
per cohort *and* state. That is, calculate $N^{\text{mult}}_{s,c}$, the number of
multiple-encounter histories first captured on occasion $c$ in state $s$ (and the similarly
defined $N^{\text{single}}_{s,c}$) for all first capture occasions $c = 1, \cdots, T-1$
and states $s = 1,2$.

#### Stan code

As in the single state case, most of the Stan code is recycled from the initial model,
including the entire functions block. The only changes to the other blocks are

i. Add the numbers $N^{\text{mult}}_{s,c}$ and $N^{\text{single}}_{s,c}$ to the
`data` block.
ii. Add the residency parameters to the `parameters` block. 
iii. In the model block, add priors for the residency parameters and increment the 
log-posterior with the relevant terms. 

The Stan code is
```stan
functions {
  matrix get_multinomial_probs(
    data int T,
    array[] vector p,
    array[] vector phi,
    array[] vector m
  ) {
    // ... function body exactly as in the initial model ...
}

data {
  int<lower=2> T;                                 // number of years
  // m-array from multiple-encounter histories alone
  array[2*(T-1), 2*(T-1)+1] int<lower=0> marr;    
  // no. single- and multiple-encounter histories per cohort and state
  array[2, T-1] int<lower=0> Nsingle;  
  array[2, T-1] int<lower=0> Nmult;  
}

parameters {
  array[2] vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T] p;        // detection probabilities
  array[2] vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T-1] phi;    // survival probabilities
  array[2] vector<lower=0,upper=1>[T-1] pi_r;   // residency probabilities
  array[2] simplex[2] m;                        // movement probabilities 
}

model {
  // calculate multinomial probabilities
  matrix[2*(T-1), 2*(T-1)+1] pr;
  pr = get_multinomial_probs( T, p, phi, m );

  // likelihood...
  // ... for indiv recaptured at least once
  for (i in 1:(2*(T-1))) {
    marr[i] ~ multinomial(pr[i]');
  }
  for (t in 1:(T-1)) {
    for (s in 1:2) {
      target += Nmult[s,t] * log(pi_r[s,t]);
    }
  }
  // ... for indiv never recaptured 
  for (t in 1:(T-1)) {
    for (s in 1:2) {
      int i = s+2*(t-1);   // indexes row s in block t
      target += Nsingle[s,t] * log( pr[i][2*(T-1)+1] * pi_r[s,t] + (1 - pi_r[s,t]) );
    }
  }
}

```

:::{.callout-caution}
Care is required with indexing to correctly select the probability of a single
encounter history for an individual of a given cohort and first capture state, 
conditional on residency.
:::
 
The m-array (and its cell probabilities) are arranged in $2 \times 2$ blocks, where
each block corresponds to an occasion of release and next recapture. Within these
blocks the rows and columns correspond to the states at release and recapture. So, for example,
an individual released on occasion $t=3$ from state $s=1$ will have the probability of it's 
various outcomes contained in row $s + 2(t-1) = 5$ of the matrix `pr` containging
the multinomial cell probabilities. The probability of the outcome 'never recaptured'
is in the last column of the matrix.
